text: Pitch is not something that physically exists in a sound wave. It is something the auditory system extracts — a perceptual decision about what the fundamental is, made by pattern-matching across partial frequencies that may not include the fundamental at all.

The phenomenon of the missing fundamental is one of the clearest demonstrations that pitch is a percept, not a measurement. Remove the lowest partial from a complex tone and listeners still report hearing the same pitch. The auditory system infers what is not there.

Bells are strange instruments precisely because their partials are inharmonic — they do not follow the integer-ratio spacing of a normal harmonic series. The result is that a bell does not have a single clear pitch; it has several competing pitch percepts that fuse imperfectly and then decay at different rates.

Helmholtz's theory of consonance was built on beating — the acoustic interference between adjacent partials. Two pure tones close in frequency produce rapid amplitude fluctuations; Helmholtz argued this roughness is what dissonance feels like. The theory is elegant but incomplete.

Plomp and Levelt revised Helmholtz by showing that roughness has a spatial component on the basilar membrane — two partials are rough when they fall within a critical band, and smooth when they are separated beyond it. The Plomp-Levelt curve maps this transition, and it is not as simple as Helmholtz assumed.

I find it fascinating that the roughness model does not perfectly predict what musicians actually hear as dissonant. The Plomp-Levelt curve is a psychoacoustic fact, but musicians work with harmonic context, not isolated intervals in a vacuum.

Auditory fusion is the process by which the auditory system groups simultaneous partials into a single perceived object. When that grouping succeeds cleanly, you hear one note. When it fails or becomes ambiguous, you hear either multiple pitches or something that resists being called pitched at all.

The limit of pitch perception is not a hard boundary — it is a gradient. As partials become more inharmonic, the pitch percept becomes progressively less stable, more multiply valued, and eventually indistinguishable from what we would simply call timbre or colour.

Spectral composers like Grisey and Murail built entire harmonic languages out of this perceptual ambiguity. A chord composed of the partials of a low brass tone, stretched across the full orchestra, hovers at the boundary between chord and timbre. You cannot decide whether you are hearing harmony or texture.

The timbral chord is not a metaphor. If you take a sine-tone decomposition of a cello note and score each partial to a separate instrument, the result is a chord that, at low dynamic levels, fuses into something that sounds more like one rich sound than like ten separate voices. Spectral fusion is a real perceptual event.

Beating between partials is measurable, but the subjective sensation of roughness is not simply proportional to beating rate. At very high beating rates, the roughness sensation disappears and the two tones fuse into one with a particular timbre. The perceptual boundary between beating and fusion is itself context-dependent.

The inharmonic partials of a gong do not prevent listeners from assigning it a pitch — players and composers speak casually about the pitch of a gong. What they mean is the most salient pitch percept, which may be weakly defined and dependent on the attack transient in ways that are hard to pin down.

Pitch as percept means that the same physical sound can be heard differently by different listeners, or by the same listener in different contexts. This is not an error or a failure of perception — it is what the category of pitch actually is. A physical correlate exists, but pitch is not reducible to it.

The auditory system performs a kind of neural Fourier decomposition along the basilar membrane, separating incoming sound into frequency components before reassembling them into perceptual objects. This decomposition is never heard directly — what we hear is already a higher-level interpretation of it.

Roughness as a perceptual category sits at an interesting intersection: it is in part acoustic, in part neurological, and in part cultural. Western listeners trained on equal temperament hear certain intervals as rough that listeners from other traditions hear as neutral or even pleasant.

What does it mean for a chord to fuse into a timbre? I think it means that the listener stops assigning the partials to separate sources and begins hearing them as properties of a single source. Auditory fusion is the perceptual decision to collapse multiplicity into unity.

Helmholtz identified roughness as the perceptual correlate of dissonance, but this implies that dissonance is a property of sound rather than of musical context. The counter-evidence is everywhere: a major seventh that is dissonant in one harmonic context is perfectly consonant in another. Roughness is necessary but not sufficient.

The Plomp-Levelt curve gives you a prediction of roughness for pairs of pure tones. Real musical instruments do not produce pure tones. Applying the curve to complex tones requires summing over all pairwise partial interactions, and this sum does not always agree with what listeners report hearing.

Spectral music asks what happens when you take the acoustics of sound production seriously as a compositional principle. Not as a surface metaphor, but as a generator. The partials of a French horn note become the pitches distributed across an ensemble — the instrument's acoustic identity becomes the score.

Whether a dense cluster of very close pitches is heard as a chord or as a single dense texture depends on the spacing, the dynamics, the reverb environment, and the listener's attentional set. The perceptual boundary is not a property of the sounds alone.

The concept of inharmonic partials becomes genuinely important in electroacoustic music, where synthesis methods like FM and ring modulation routinely produce spectra with no harmonic relationship to any fundamental. Determining the pitch of an FM tone is often ambiguous in ways that acoustic instruments rarely achieve.

Auditory fusion explains why a piano is heard as a single source even though it is simultaneously excited at many partials across a complex, slightly inharmonic spectrum. The auditory system treats the co-onset of related partials as strong evidence for common origin, and fuses accordingly.

There is a version of the perceptual boundary question that gets raised in ethnomusicology: listeners acculturated to different tuning systems hear the same interval as more or less rough. This suggests that the Plomp-Levelt curve is a baseline, not a ceiling — cultural learning adjusts where the roughness feels salient.

Beating occurs when two tones are too close in frequency for the auditory system to resolve them into separate critical bands. This critical band width is itself frequency-dependent — it is wider at low frequencies and narrower at high. The roughness landscape is not uniform across the pitch register.

The spectral fusion that Grisey exploited is not a new phenomenon — it is what string orchestras have always exploited when they sustain a single pitch across many instruments. Thirty violins produce a richer sound than one not only in volume but in spectral complexity. The orchestration is already a kind of timbral composition.

Pitch as a percept fails gracefully rather than catastrophically when partials become inharmonic. The listener does not simply hear chaos — they hear a degraded, multiply-valued, ambiguous pitch that can still support some melodic reasoning. The system is robust to inharmonicity in a way that no strict definition of pitch would predict.

One thing I find underappreciated about the roughness model is that it predicts not just which intervals are rough but by how much. The Plomp-Levelt curve has a shape — roughness rises steeply at the lower semitone boundary and falls gradually above the critical band. That asymmetry has compositional implications.

A timbral chord is structurally distinct from a normal chord even if the two are built from identical pitches. If the pitches of a timbral chord are derived from the harmonic series of a sub-fundamental, they have a convergent structure — they imply a missing root — whereas an arbitrary chord does not.

Helmholtz was working before the anatomy of the inner ear was well understood. He proposed that different hair cells responded to different frequencies, which turned out to be broadly correct, but he did not know about the active mechanics of the cochlea or the role of olivocochlear feedback. His roughness theory predates a lot of the machinery that would be needed to complete it.

The spectral composers made an implicit argument: if the distinction between a chord and a timbre is only perceptual, then the tools of harmony and the tools of orchestration are not categorically different. They are both ways of shaping how partial frequencies distribute across the audible field.

Inharmonic partials occur naturally in percussion instruments, in bells, in wooden bars, in metal tubes. The fact that Western art music has traditionally centred pitched instruments with harmonic spectra is itself a cultural selection — the acoustic richness of inharmonic instruments was consigned to special structural roles rather than being explored as primary material.

The perceptual boundary between pitch and timbre is not fixed — it shifts with attention. A listener attending to the pitch of a clarinet note places the boundary differently than a listener attending to the difference between a clarinet and an oboe playing the same note. The boundary is a function of the perceptual task, not of the sound.

Auditory scene analysis, the broader framework that includes auditory fusion, treats hearing as a problem-solving activity: the auditory system is trying to infer the sources that produced the mixture of vibrations arriving at the ear. Pitch is one cue it uses; onset time, harmonicity, and spatial location are others.

The Plomp-Levelt curve does not predict musical dissonance for complex tones without summing over all partial pairs. When you actually do that computation for a major triad in close position, the total roughness is low. For a minor second in close position, it is high. The psychoacoustic predictions mostly agree with musical intuition, but not always.

What would a compositional practice look like if it took the perceptual boundary between pitch and timbre as its central subject? Spectral music is one answer. There are others — noise music, drone music, microtonality all probe different parts of that boundary from different directions.

Beating at a moderate rate — around 20-30 Hz — produces a sensation that is recognisably roughness. Very slow beating — 1-2 Hz — produces a gentle, almost pleasant undulation that musicians call vibrato when controlled. The beating phenomenon spans a perceptual range from ornament to unpleasantness depending only on rate.

The spectral fusion of orchestra and sound design is now well understood enough to be industrialised — film music composers routinely blur the line between a sustained orchestral chord and synthetic texture. What Grisey made strange, commercial practice has made ordinary. The conceptual edge has moved.

Pitch as percept is a special case of object perception generally. The auditory system constructs a perceptual object — a pitch — from cues that are individually insufficient to determine it. This is the same process by which vision constructs a face from gradients of light. There is no face in the light; there is no pitch in the wave.

The distinction between a dense cluster of close pitches and a single timbre is ultimately a distinction between two modes of auditory organisation. The same acoustic material can cross that line depending on register, dynamic, ensemble, and listening context. Spectral composers exploit this crossing as a compositional device.

Inharmonic partials in a bell do not simply make the pitch ambiguous — they make it time-varying. Different partials decay at different rates, so the pitch percept of a bell actually shifts as the sound rings down. The pitch is not just multiply valued; it is a moving target.

Roughness is an aversive sensation for most listeners, but this is not universal and it is not static. Musicians who work extensively with extended techniques or electroacoustic music report recalibrated roughness thresholds — what was once uncomfortable becomes neutral or interesting. Perceptual categories adapt.

The auditory system's fusion of harmonic partials into a single pitch percept is remarkably robust. You can remove several partials from a harmonic series, add noise, or shift the fundamental slightly, and the pitch percept persists. This robustness is what allows musical instruments to be heard clearly in reverberant acoustic environments.

Helmholtz's work in On the Sensations of Tone is sometimes treated as quaint because it predates neurophysiology. But his core insight — that harmonic consonance is related to the relationship between upper partials, not just fundamentals — remains structurally correct. The mechanism he proposed was wrong; the level of analysis was right.

Spectral music raised a genuine challenge to the concept of atonality. If you build a harmonic language from the overtone series, you are not tonal in a functional sense, but you are not atonal either — you have a kind of acoustic grounding that twelve-tone serialism deliberately lacks. It occupies a previously unnamed position.

The timbral chord and the normal chord differ in their implied source structure. A normal chord implies multiple independent sources; a timbral chord implies one source with a complex internal structure. Listeners may not consciously make this inference, but it may still shape how they hear the harmony as stable or unstable.

Whether the pitch-timbre boundary is fixed or context-dependent is not merely a perceptual question — it is a compositional question. A composer who treats it as fixed is working with stable categories. A composer who treats it as moveable is working with the boundary itself as material.

The Plomp-Levelt curve was derived from experiments on isolated pairs of pure tones heard by trained and untrained listeners in anechoic conditions. Almost nothing about the typical musical listening situation matches those experimental conditions. The curve tells you about roughness in its most controlled form, not in its ecological context.

Auditory fusion depends heavily on common onset: partials that begin at the same moment are more readily grouped together into a single perceived object. This is why the attack transient of an instrument is so important for its perceptual identity — without a shared onset, the same spectral content is heard as a chord rather than a note.

The perceptual question of where pitch ends and timbre begins is asymmetric. Thinning a complex tone down to a pure sine leaves pitch but removes all timbre. Adding inharmonic partials to a pure sine adds timbre while degrading the pitch. The two qualities trade off, but not symmetrically.

There is something philosophically interesting about the fact that pitch — the most fundamental category of musical organisation — turns out to be a perceptual construction rather than a physical feature. Music is organised around something the auditory system invents. The order is not in the sound; it is in the listening.
